canonical_topic: Hydrocarbon gas liquids: alkanes versus alkenes
definition: NGLs belong to the broader category of hydrocarbon gas liquids (HGLs), which splits into alkanes (paraffins — the NGLs proper) and alkenes (olefins — petrochemical feedstock products).
core_idea: Alkanes have single covalent bonds between carbon atoms while alkenes have one or more double bonds, giving alkenes fewer hydrogen atoms for the same carbon count; alkenes serve as feedstock for plastics, artificial rubber, paints, and solvents.
key_points: Alkenes (olefins) = feedstock products for plastics/rubber/paint/solvent manufacturing.
Chemical distinction: alkenes have double carbon-carbon bonds and thus fewer hydrogen atoms than alkanes with the same carbon count.
relationships: Alkanes and alkenes are both HGLs but differ in bonding and downstream use
trading_implications: There is no major trading market for refinery/petrochemical feedstocks (alkenes) — from a trading perspective it's mostly enough to know they exist.
caveats: Alkenes/olefins are sometimes lumped in with tradeable NGLs, but the author notes they aren't meaningfully traded as a market.
